name: Money Illusion
description: People often judge money by its face value rather than its real purchasing power. Nominal numbers can feel like gains or losses even when the underlying economic value says otherwise.
design_relevance_note: Most relevant to pricing, salary/compensation communication, inflation-era messaging, subscriptions, discounts, and any interface that frames value in nominal terms users may treat as psychologically real.
prevalence_note: A standard term in behavioral economics and pricing/inflation commentary, but only intermittently named in mainstream product-design discourse outside commerce or fintech contexts.

findings.description: An empirical analysis of Treasury bill, safe-stock, and risky-stock pricing found support for the hypothesis that the stock market itself suffers from money illusion -- discounting real cash flows at nominal interest rates rather than adjusting for inflation. By simultaneously examining all three asset classes, the study could distinguish genuine money illusion from a mere change in investor risk attitudes. A genuine, high-stakes, real-world extension of money illusion from individual judgment tasks (the original 1997 paradigm) into aggregate financial-market pricing.
findings.source_title: Money Illusion in the Stock Market: The Modigliani-Cohn Hypothesis

findings.description: People evaluated wage and price changes using nominal face values rather than real purchasing power, treating nominal cuts as unfair while accepting nominal raises during inflation even when both implied equivalent real losses.
